title: Tyson Foods Shrinks Beef Operations as Historic Cattle Shortage Forces Industry-Wide Plant Closures
excerpt: The nation's largest meat processor is closing multiple beef plants and expects up to $650 million in losses as U.S. cattle herds hit a 75-year low, with rivals JBS and Cargill also shuttering facilities.
body:
• Tyson Foods is closing beef plants in Illinois, Utah, and Nebraska while pursuing the sale of a Washington facility, concentrating operations at two remaining mega-plants.
  • The U.S. cattle herd has fallen to its lowest level in 75 years, driven by prolonged drought, elevated feed costs, and a flesh-eating parasite that has halted Mexican cattle imports.
  • Tyson's beef unit lost $142 million last quarter and now expects $500 million to $650 million in operating losses for fiscal 2026.
  • Industry rivals JBS and Cargill have also closed multiple facilities, with more than 5,000 workers across the sector losing jobs in recent months.

Tyson Foods is taking a meat cleaver to its beef-processing network as the worst U.S. cattle shortage in decades continues to squeeze margins across the industry, announcing the closure of its beef plant in Joslin, Illinois, and a case-ready facility in Eagle Mountain, Utah, while pursuing the sale of its Pasco, Washington, plant.

The moves, announced on Aug. 14, follow the meatpacker's previously announced closure of its massive Lexington, Nebraska, plant — which employed more than 3,200 workers and could process 5,000 head of cattle daily — and its decision to slash production at its Amarillo, Texas, facility to a single shift.

A Shrinking Footprint

Tyson said it will concentrate beef operations around its facilities in Dakota City, Nebraska, and Holcomb, Kansas, with plans to restore shifts at Amarillo as cattle supplies eventually improve. Management has argued the firm can offset the closures by processing more cattle at fewer locations, keeping overall slaughter volume roughly unchanged.

Investors appeared to welcome the restructuring, with Tyson shares rising about 3% following the announcement. But the numbers underscore the severity of the crisis. The company's beef unit lost $142 million in its latest quarter, while cattle costs surged $525 million from a year earlier. Although beef prices rose nearly 12%, volume fell 16%.

Tyson now expects its beef segment to post an adjusted operating loss of $500 million to $650 million in fiscal 2026, significantly worse than its previous forecast of $350 million to $500 million.

"These decisions are never easy because they directly affect our team members and the communities where we operate."

— Wesley Batista Filho, JBS USA CEO

An Industry-Wide Crisis

Tyson is far from alone. JBS, the world's largest meat processing company, announced in June that it would close its beef-processing plant in Souderton, Pennsylvania — affecting 1,485 workers — along with a value-added facility in Memphis and a Pilgrim's Pride poultry plant in Chattanooga, Tennessee. Together, JBS's closures and restructuring are set to impact more than 2,000 workers.

Cargill permanently closed its beef processing facility in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, earlier this year, cutting 221 jobs. American Foods Group shuttered its Skylark Meats plant in Omaha, eliminating 218 positions. Combined with the Tyson layoffs in Nebraska, more than 4,000 food-manufacturing jobs have been lost in Nebraska alone since late 2025.

The Root Cause: A Vanishing Herd

The U.S. cattle herd has dropped to its lowest level in nearly 75 years, according to the USDA, after years of persistent drought that dried up grazing pastures and elevated feed costs pushed ranchers to shrink their herds. Beef cow numbers were down 1% from a year earlier as of July, while the 2026 calf crop is expected to be 2% smaller.

The New World screwworm — a flesh-eating parasite — has added further complications. The U.S. suspended imports of Mexican cattle more than a year ago to prevent the pest's spread. Mexico normally supplies roughly one million animals annually. The parasite has since reached the U.S., prompting quarantines and movement restrictions.

The USDA plans to begin reopening one Arizona port to Mexican cattle on Aug. 24, but imports will resume gradually. Tyson CEO Donnie King has said increased imports could provide some relief in 2027 and beyond, but imported calves still need to be raised and fattened before they reach processing plants.

Consumers Feel the Pinch

The supply crunch is hitting consumers directly. Beef and veal prices were 14.8% higher in April 2026 than a year earlier, according to the USDA, which expects beef prices to rise 12.1% for the full year — well above the 3.2% increase forecast for overall grocery prices. Farm-level cattle prices surged 17.7% over the same period.

The widening gap between beef and poultry prices — chicken was up just 0.5% — is pushing more consumers toward cheaper proteins and putting additional pressure on the beef industry's already strained economics.

No Quick Fix

Because cattle take years to breed and raise, supplies are likely to remain tight even as ranchers begin rebuilding. Meatpackers face a stark reality: there are simply not enough animals to keep all their plants running efficiently, and competition for scarce cattle continues to push up procurement costs.

For Tyson, the restructuring signals that management is no longer waiting for the beef market to fix itself. If cattle supplies eventually recover, the company could process more animals through fewer, more efficient plants — potentially accelerating its return to profitability. But analysts caution that any meaningful supply recovery remains years away.
